hsc-2021 - question preview

34 questions in the main set, 1 quarantined. Correct answers are highlighted green. This is a static QC preview, not the live app.

Main set

#1true-falsefrom Q1inquiry 5.1
A marble is rolled off the edge of a horizontal bench and falls to the floor. Rolling the marble off at a slower speed would make it land closer to the base of the bench, but it would still take the same time to reach the floor.
  • ✓ True
  • False
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): The time of flight depends only on the height of the bench; the launch speed only affects the horizontal range.
#2word-bankfrom Q2inquiry 6.1
A positive charge moves to the right through a uniform electric field that points up the page. The electric force on the charge is directed ___ the page, because the force on a positive charge is ___ to the field and does not depend on the charge's velocity.
A positive charge moves to the right through a uniform electric field that points up the page. The electric force on the charge is directed up the page, because the force on a positive charge is parallel to the field and does not depend on the charge's velocity.
Word bank
up down parallel perpendicular opposite
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): $\vec{F} = q\vec{E}$; for a positive $q$ the force is along $\vec{E}$.
#3multiple-choicefrom Q3inquiry 8.5
Which of the following is NOT a fundamental particle in the Standard Model of matter?
  • ✓ Proton
  • Electron
  • Gluon
  • Muon
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): A proton is made of quarks; the electron and muon are leptons, and the gluon is a force-carrying boson.
#4word-bankfrom Q3binquiry 8.5
In the Standard Model, the proton is not a fundamental particle because it is made of three ___.
In the Standard Model, the proton is not a fundamental particle because it is made of three quarks.
Word bank
quarks leptons gluons photons
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): A proton is two up quarks and one down quark.
#5multiple-choicefrom Q4inquiry 7.4
An astronaut travels towards Earth at 0.8c and sends radio pulses to an observer on Earth at regular intervals. Which quantity would the astronaut and the Earth observer measure to be the same?
  • ✓ The speed of the radio pulses
  • The length of the spaceship
  • The momentum of the astronaut
  • The time interval between the radio pulses
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): The speed of light (and of any electromagnetic wave) is the same for all inertial observers; length, time intervals and momentum are all frame-dependent.
#6drag-dropfrom Q5inquiry 7.1
2021-q5-stellar-spectrum.png
The spectrum shown is a broad continuous distribution of intensity crossed by several sharp dark dips (the features labelled Y). Match each description to what the spectrum shows.
Most likely source of this spectrum→A star
The features labelled Y→Absorption lines
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): A continuous spectrum with dark gaps is produced when light from a hot dense source passes through a cooler gas, as in a star's atmosphere.
#7true-falsefrom Q5binquiry 7.1
The pattern of dark absorption lines in a star's spectrum can be used to identify which chemical elements are present in the star's outer layers.
  • ✓ True
  • False
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Each element absorbs light at its own characteristic set of wavelengths.
#8word-bankfrom Q6inquiry 8.1
2021-q6-pp-chain.png
In the part of the proton-proton chain shown, two protons fuse to form a deuterium nucleus (plus a positron and a neutrino). The deuterium nucleus then fuses with another proton to form isotope R plus a gamma ray. Isotope R is ___.
In the part of the proton-proton chain shown, two protons fuse to form a deuterium nucleus (plus a positron and a neutrino). The deuterium nucleus then fuses with another proton to form isotope R plus a gamma ray. Isotope R is He-3.
Word bank
He-3 H-2 He-2 H-3
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Deuterium (1 proton, 1 neutron) plus a proton gives a nucleus with 2 protons and 1 neutron.
#9true-falsefrom Q6binquiry 8.1
The overall effect of the proton-proton chain in a star is that four hydrogen nuclei are converted into one helium-4 nucleus, with a release of energy.
  • ✓ True
  • False
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): The helium-4 nucleus has slightly less mass than the four protons; the difference is released as energy.
#10drag-dropfrom Q7inquiry 6.3
In an ideal transformer, the current in the secondary coil is four times as large as the current in the primary coil. Match each property to the correct description.
Type of transformer→Step-down
Ratio of primary turns to secondary turns→4 : 1
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): For an ideal transformer $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$, so a larger secondary current means a smaller secondary voltage (step-down) and fewer secondary turns.
#11numeric-entryfrom Q7binquiry 6.3
An ideal transformer has 800 turns on the primary coil and 200 turns on the secondary coil. The primary current is 0.50 A. Calculate the secondary current.
2.0A
accepted within ±2% (relative)
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): For an ideal transformer, $\dfrac{I_s}{I_p} = \dfrac{N_p}{N_s}$.
#12word-bankfrom Q8inquiry 7.2
2021-q8-poisson-spot.png
Light from a point source shines on a small circular metal disc, and a bright spot appears at the very centre of the disc's shadow on the screen, as shown. This bright spot is produced by the ___ of light waves around the edge of the disc, followed by their constructive ___ at the centre of the shadow.
Light from a point source shines on a small circular metal disc, and a bright spot appears at the very centre of the disc's shadow on the screen, as shown. This bright spot is produced by the diffraction of light waves around the edge of the disc, followed by their constructive interference at the centre of the shadow.
Word bank
diffraction interference refraction polarisation reflection
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Every point on the disc's rim is the same distance from the centre of the shadow, so the diffracted waves arrive there in phase.
#13true-falsefrom Q8binquiry 7.2
The bright spot at the centre of a circular object's shadow is strong evidence for the wave model of light and cannot be explained by treating light purely as particles.
  • ✓ True
  • False
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Only waves diffract around an obstacle and interfere constructively behind it.
#14multiple-choicefrom Q9inquiry 5.3
2021-q9-mass-two-stars.png
A mass M moves along a straight path that starts on one side of a pair of identical stars, passes midway between them, and continues out the other side to position X, as shown. How does the gravitational potential energy U of the mass change during this movement?
  • ✓ U decreases to a minimum as M passes between the stars, then increases again
  • U increases steadily throughout the movement
  • U decreases steadily throughout the movement
  • U stays constant because M is always equidistant from the two stars
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): The mass is closest to the stars (deepest in the combined potential well, so U most negative) as it passes the midpoint.
#15true-falsefrom Q9binquiry 5.3
2021-q9-mass-two-stars.png
As the mass M in the diagram moves from far away towards the point midway between the two stars, its gravitational potential energy becomes more negative.
  • ✓ True
  • False
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Moving closer to the stars means moving deeper into the gravitational potential well.
#16multiple-choicefrom Q10inquiry 6.4
2021-q10-magnet-copper-block.png
A strong magnet is moved to the right at constant speed past a stationary copper block, as shown. What is the direction of the force acting on the copper block?
  • ✓ To the right (the same direction the magnet is moving)
  • To the left (opposite to the magnet's motion)
  • Into the page
  • Out of the page
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Eddy currents induced in the copper oppose the change in flux (Lenz's law), which drags the block along in the direction of the magnet's motion.
#17true-falsefrom Q10binquiry 6.4
2021-q10-magnet-copper-block.png
The eddy currents induced in the copper block by the passing magnet exert a force on the block that acts in the same direction as the magnet's motion.
  • ✓ True
  • False
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): By Lenz's law the induced effects oppose the relative motion, so the block is dragged after the magnet.
#18numeric-entryfrom Q11inquiry 7.3
Calculate the peak wavelength of the electromagnetic radiation emitted by a person whose body temperature is 310 K. Use Wien's displacement law $\lambda_{max} T = b$ with $b = 2.90 \times 10^{-3}$ m K.
9.35e-06m
accepted within ±3% (relative)
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): $\lambda_{max} = b / T$. The answer is in the infrared.
#19numeric-entryfrom Q11binquiry 7.3
A star has a surface temperature of 5800 K. Calculate the wavelength at which it emits maximum intensity. Use Wien's displacement law $\lambda_{max} T = b$ with $b = 2.90 \times 10^{-3}$ m K.
5e-07m
accepted within ±3% (relative)
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): This wavelength (about 500 nm) is in the visible part of the spectrum.
#20word-bankfrom Q12inquiry 5.2
The magnitude of the back EMF induced in a DC motor is ___ proportional to the motor's angular velocity.
The magnitude of the back EMF induced in a DC motor is directly proportional to the motor's angular velocity.
Word bank
directly inversely exponentially not
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Faster rotation cuts field lines more quickly, inducing a larger opposing EMF; a graph of back EMF against angular velocity is a straight line through the origin.
#21multiple-choicefrom Q13inquiry 8.3
2021-q13-bohr-transitions.png
The diagram shows electron transitions W, X, Y and Z in a Bohr-model hydrogen atom (W: n=2 to n=1; X: n=4 to n=1; Y: n=3 to n=2; Z: n=5 to n=2). Which transition produces light of the shortest wavelength?
  • ✓ X
  • W
  • Y
  • Z
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Shortest wavelength means the largest photon energy, so look for the transition with the biggest energy gap.
#22word-bankfrom Q13binquiry 8.3
2021-q13-bohr-transitions.png
For light emitted when an electron drops between two energy levels, a shorter wavelength corresponds to a ___ energy difference between the levels.
For light emitted when an electron drops between two energy levels, a shorter wavelength corresponds to a larger energy difference between the levels.
Word bank
larger smaller negative zero
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$: smaller $\lambda$ means larger $E$.
#23multiple-choicefrom Q14inquiry 5.3
Which statement correctly describes the gravitational interaction between the Earth and the Moon?
  • ✓ The Earth accelerates towards the Moon
  • The net force acting on the Earth is zero
  • The Moon and the Earth experience equal and opposite accelerations
  • The gravitational force acting on the Moon is smaller than the force acting on the Earth
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): The forces on the two bodies are equal in magnitude (Newton's third law), but the Earth's much greater mass gives it a much smaller acceleration -- small, but not zero.
#24true-falsefrom Q14binquiry 5.3
The gravitational force the Moon exerts on the Earth is equal in magnitude to the force the Earth exerts on the Moon, but the Earth's resulting acceleration is much smaller because of its far greater mass.
  • ✓ True
  • False
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Equal forces (Newton's third law), unequal masses, so unequal accelerations.
#25multiple-choicefrom Q15inquiry 7.2
Unpolarised light passes through two polarisers. The transmission axis of the second polariser is fixed. $I_1$ is the intensity after the first polariser and $I_2$ is the intensity after the second. If the transmission axis of the first polariser is rotated, how are $I_1$ and $I_2$ affected?
  • ✓ Only $I_2$ changes
  • Both $I_1$ and $I_2$ change
  • Only $I_1$ changes
  • Neither $I_1$ nor $I_2$ changes
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Unpolarised light loses exactly half its intensity through any single polariser, so $I_1$ is fixed; but rotating the first polariser changes the angle between the two axes, which changes $I_2$.
#26true-falsefrom Q15binquiry 7.2
When initially unpolarised light passes through a single polariser, the transmitted intensity is always half the incident intensity, regardless of how the polariser is oriented.
  • ✓ True
  • False
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Unpolarised light contains all polarisation directions equally, so on average half gets through.
#27numeric-entryfrom Q16inquiry 7.4
The Sun has an energy output of $3.85 \times 10^{28}$ W. Using $E = mc^2$ with $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$, calculate the decrease in the Sun's mass each minute.
25700000000000.0kg
accepted within ±3% (relative)
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Energy radiated in one minute is $3.85 \times 10^{28} \times 60$ J; divide by $c^2$.
#28numeric-entryfrom Q16binquiry 7.4
The Sun radiates energy at $3.85 \times 10^{28}$ W. Using $E = mc^2$ with $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$, calculate the rate at which the Sun loses mass, in kg per second.
428000000000.0kg s^{-1}
accepted within ±3% (relative)
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Divide the power (energy per second) by $c^2$.
#29multiple-choicefrom Q17inquiry 6.2
Two long horizontal parallel conductors X and Y are part of the same series circuit with an AC supply and a light bulb, so the current always flows in opposite directions in the two conductors. X hangs directly below Y, each supported by a spring balance. Which statement correctly compares the forces the balances measure?
  • ✓ The force measured on X is always greater than or equal to the force measured on Y
  • The forces measured on X and Y are always equal
  • The force measured on Y is always greater than or equal to the force measured on X
  • Which measured force is greater reverses continually
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Opposite currents means the wires always repel, so X (below) is always pushed down (balance reads more) and Y (above) is always pushed up (balance reads less). The strength varies with the AC but the direction does not.
#30true-falsefrom Q17binquiry 6.2
Because conductors X and Y are in the same series circuit, their currents are always in opposite directions, so the wires repel each other at every instant of the AC cycle (except when the current is momentarily zero).
  • ✓ True
  • False
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Anti-parallel currents always repel; reversing both currents together does not change that.
#31multiple-choicefrom Q19inquiry 8.4
Rh-106 is a beta-emitting radioisotope with a half-life of 30 seconds. A sample is placed near an electrode in an evacuated chamber connected to a galvanometer and a variable DC supply. With the supply at zero, a current I flows (from the beta particles reaching the electrode). The stopping voltage $V_s$ (the voltage needed to reduce this current to zero) is also measured. The measurements are repeated a few minutes later. How do the two sets of measurements compare?
  • ✓ Only I changes
  • Only $V_s$ changes
  • Both I and $V_s$ change
  • Neither I nor $V_s$ changes
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): After several half-lives the activity (rate of beta emission) has dropped a lot, so I falls; but the maximum energy of the beta particles is fixed by the decay, so $V_s$ is unchanged.
#32true-falsefrom Q19binquiry 8.4
As a radioactive sample decays over several half-lives, the rate at which it emits beta particles falls, but the maximum kinetic energy of those beta particles stays the same.
  • ✓ True
  • False
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): The maximum beta energy is set by the decay's energy release, which does not change; only the number of decays per second falls.
#33word-bankfrom Q20inquiry 5.2
Photoelectrons freed from a metal (work function $\phi$) by photons of energy $2\phi$ travel in a circular path of radius $r$ in a magnetic field. The path radius is proportional to $\sqrt{E_k}$, where $E_k$ is the electron's kinetic energy. If the photon energy is doubled to $4\phi$, the maximum path radius changes by a factor of ___.
Photoelectrons freed from a metal (work function $\phi$) by photons of energy $2\phi$ travel in a circular path of radius $r$ in a magnetic field. The path radius is proportional to $\sqrt{E_k}$, where $E_k$ is the electron's kinetic energy. If the photon energy is doubled to $4\phi$, the maximum path radius changes by a factor of $\sqrt{3}$.
Word bank
$\sqrt{3}$ $\sqrt{2}$ 2 3
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): With photon energy $2\phi$, $E_k = \phi$. With photon energy $4\phi$, $E_k = 3\phi$. The radius ratio is $\sqrt{3\phi / \phi}$.
#34true-falsefrom Q20binquiry 5.2
For a photoelectron moving in a circle in a magnetic field, the radius of the circular path is proportional to the square root of the photoelectron's kinetic energy.
  • ✓ True
  • False
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$ and $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, so $r \propto v \propto \sqrt{E_k}$.

#Q1multiple-choicefrom Q18inquiry 5.1
An evacuated chamber contains two vertical parallel plates connected to a power supply through a switch that is initially closed. A positive charge falls under gravity from a point near the top, between the plates. While the switch is closed the charge follows a path that curves towards one plate. When the charge has fallen halfway down, the switch is opened (disconnecting the plates from the supply but leaving them charged). Which best describes the rest of the trajectory?
  • ✓ It keeps curving towards the same plate, because the isolated plates retain their charge and the field between them is unchanged
  • It becomes a straight line, because opening the switch removes the field
  • It curves back towards the other plate
  • It falls straight down, because gravity is now the only force
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): An isolated (disconnected) charged capacitor holds its charge, so its field does not change.
Quarantine reason: The original is a 'which of these four trajectory diagrams' question (option images), and the key answer is A. I have reworded it above to a self-contained MCQ whose correct answer (field persists after the switch opens because the plates are an isolated capacitor, so the path keeps curving the same way) is the standard HSC physics -- but I cannot verify from the extracted text that NESA's diagram A actually shows 'keeps curving the same way' rather than, say, 'curve then straight line'. Please confirm against the paper's option diagrams, then this can move into the main set as-is; or supply a single combined image of the four labelled trajectories to keep it as an A/B/C/D question; or approve dropping it.
